subject: Archaeology
title: The Uluburun Shipwreck
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Uluburun Shipwreck usable.

hook.text: A sponge diver off Turkey found the richest ancient shipwreck ever — a 3,300-year-old floating department store.

buildup.text: The Uluburun wreck carried copper, tin, gold, ivory, amber, ebony, and glass from at least seven different cultures.

discovery.text: One ton of tin and ten tons of copper were on board — enough to make 300 bronze weapons.

twist.text: A golden scarab bearing Queen Nefertiti's name was among the cargo.

climax.text: The wreck proved that Bronze Age trade networks were far more connected and sophisticated than anyone had imagined.

punchline.text: One sunken ship rewrote the Bronze Age. The sea kept the evidence for 3,300 years.

quiz.question: What did the Uluburun shipwreck reveal about the Bronze Age?
options: Maritime trade did not exist before the Iron Age
Trade networks were far more connected and sophisticated than previously imagined
Only the Egyptians were capable of long-distance sea voyages

details.summary: The Uluburun shipwreck off Turkey, dating to around 1300 BCE, carried cargo from at least seven cultures — Canaanite, Mycenaean, Egyptian, Cypriot, Kassite, Nubian, and Assyrian. Its diverse cargo of copper, tin, glass, gold, and ivory reveals the vast scale of Late Bronze Age international trade.
details.whyItMatters: Uluburun proved that the Late Bronze Age had a globalized trading network connecting the entire eastern Mediterranean and beyond. A single ship carried the products of seven civilizations, overturning the idea that ancient trade was simple and local.
takeaways: The Uluburun wreck dates to around 1300 BCE off Turkey
Cargo from seven cultures proves vast Bronze Age trade networks
It carried copper, tin, glass, gold, ivory, and luxury goods

faq.question: What was the most significant cargo on the Uluburun ship?
faq.answer: Ten tons of copper and one ton of tin — exactly the 10:1 ratio needed to make bronze. This single cargo could have equipped an army, revealing the industrial scale of metal trade. The ship also carried hippopotamus ivory, ebony, ostrich eggs, and a gold scarab of Nefertiti.

faq.question: How was the Uluburun wreck excavated?
faq.answer: George Bass and the Institute of Nautical Archaeology conducted 22,413 individual dives over eleven field seasons from 1984 to 1994. At a depth of 44-52 meters, divers had limited bottom time. It remains one of the most painstaking underwater excavations ever conducted.
